synopsis: Across the booklet, visually convincing scenes and improved image-quality scores do not establish sensor fidelity or equivalent detector, tracker and braking behaviour; photorealism is insufficient as validation evidence [f3711, f7071, f10554, f14790]. Radar studies illustrate the gap: RadaRays improved image similarity and produced realistic odometry, yet a detector trained on real data failed to transfer, while the 2025 wheel-loader study reported failure on most simulated cars, partly because material properties were guessed [f4826, f4423]. In a November 2025 point-cloud study, density-aware Chamfer distance correlated best with perception among the metrics compared, but real-versus-simulated scans still averaged 0.63 DCD with only 21% segmentation mIoU; whether these distributional metrics predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain [f4441, f4442, f5067]. Appearance metrics are not universally uninformative: a 2024 study found correlations with visual-odometry behaviour as gamma varied, and camera photorealism may matter, but fidelity must be selected for the sensor and tested requirement rather than ranked by screenshots [f4758, f4331]. Validation should compare withheld real raw data with simulation at sensor-output, perception, task and closed-loop levels, including TTC, trigger distance, false brakes and missed brakes; the booklet identifies function-level perception and fusion validity as a gap in its seven-question scope [f10558, f4444, f12867, f5086]. Practical checks include a pre-registered one-sensor correlation pilot and weather falsification tests against measured degradation, with good virtual metrics but rain-, dust-, night- or glare-clustered field failures treated as warning signs [f10934, f10937, f12455].
